Residents should also invest in portable power banks, solar chargers, or generator backups to extend the use of essential communication devices. Practicing communication drills with family and community members can ensure preparedness for a real emergency. Governments and emergency management agencies should implement resilient communication strategies. Deploying mobile cell towers, satellite communication units, and emergency broadcasting infrastructure can provide critical connectivity in disaster-stricken areas. Authorities should also establish emergency information hubs where residents can gather for updates, charge devices, and access resources. 42 Ultimately, maintaining communication during a grid outage requires a combination of preparation, alternative technologies, and coordinated community efforts. While digital networks are ideal when available, residents must be ready to switch to analog and offline methods when necessary. By proactively equipping individuals with the knowledge and tools needed for emergency communication, communities can ensure safety, reduce panic, and facilitate effective disaster response. Food Safety Minimum Resilience Standard: Individuals have access to fresh or nonperishable foods in their home for at least three days and are able to obtain fresh or nonperishable foods beyond three days. Community members dependent on food subsidies have clear processes for the replacement of food impacted by power outages. Vulnerability: Most vulnerable to food loss during a power outage are community members who face other financial, health, and access-related challenges. These community groups include low-income households, older individuals on a fixed income, people with disabilities or chronic illnesses that require specialized diets, families with young children, unhoused individuals, and those with traditional food access issues due to food deserts, rural areas with large distances to stores, and/or mobility-limited individuals. Community members on food assistance may experience a delay in replacing lost benefits. Potential Distributed Actions: Households can prepare by having a stock of nonperishable foods and a manual can opener for when refrigerated and frozen foods spoil. Keeping the refrigerator and freezer doors closed as much as possible will keep food cold for longer. Coolers and ice can be used to keep food from spoiling. Additionally, when the temperature is appropriate, perishables can be stored outside to stay cold. Camping stoves and fire can be used for alternative cooking methods for warm meals. Potential Shared Solutions: Distribute nonperishable foods when able. Cooking and serving perishable foods for the community to help reduce food waste and provide a resource to those struggling to access food. Additional support may be needed for individuals with food assistance as they wait for additional funds to replace food lost during a power outage. Rationale: During a power outage, keeping food safe is a major concern for both individuals and the community. Without electricity, refrigerators and freezers can only keep food at safe temperatures for a limited time, increasing the risk of spoilage and foodborne illnesses. Communities should ensure that residents have access to food safety guidelines and resources, such as emergency food distribution centers or backup refrigeration options.
